utterances.text: Well, it's obvious, according to your report, isn't it, on command and control?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My report on -- the aspects of command and control I have covered in my report do not cover the relations between the military, i.e., the HV and the police and other organs of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As you were commenting on the military and civil authority of Mr. Cermak, isn't that something you should have done as part of your analysis? Don't you think?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible, but the conclusion I drew is based on the documents that describe the role of General Cermak as the commander of the Knin Garrison. But I agree with you it could have helped just to provide background on the de jure aspects of the relations between the military as well as the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm going to look at a document now called Exhibit P46. It's a United Nations document coming from Mr. Al-Alfi's department, and it concerns the report of a meeting on the 22nd of August between the UN agencies apparent in the document as well as Mr. Romanic, chief of police for Knin, and Mr. Jukic Pavo, the officer in charge of Civil Defence in Knin. And if we turn to page 2 of this document and look at paragraph 6, we see a report that Mr. Pavo, a chemistry engineer normally based in the Civil Defence headquarters in Zagreb, and now in charge of Civil Defence in Knin, had joined the meeting that was taking place, and according to him, the main tasks of the Civil Defence in the area, he describes them, and they include removing dead animals and human bodies. And he further informed the team that the collection of dead human bodies is being carried out by a specialised team operating in the Knin area and that the people connect with it. And then in paragraph 7 we see Mr. Kostovic mentioned again, deputy prime minister who was the only Croatian official authorised to speak to the public on a question concerning burials. Again, have you seen this document? Were you aware of its information?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen this document while preparing my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm going to be cutting this section slightly shorter now than it could have been. Exhibit D351, please. This is a document from a man called Mr. Cetina. Do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and it's also stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. He's the chief of the Zadar police administration. Did you know that he filed a number of report, of which this is one, to the Ministry of Interior Main Staff which had an operation return department, and did you know those reports over many days concern the reports of the bodies found in the area of Zadar-Knin?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm familiar in general terms with the -- the staff return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. These reports started from slightly before this, on the 7th of August, 1995, and they indicate a clear reporting line, don't they, from the police in Zadar-Knin up to the Ministry of Interior in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And none of those documents included a reference to General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen the other documents, but if you talk about reference in the sense of addressees or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They've all been exhibited in the case, a large number, which if he was superior to Mr. Cetina, he would have received a copy of these reports; would he not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could, but Mr. Cetina could also have reported otherwise to Mr. Cermak. Now, I have not claimed in my report that Mr. Cermak -- or General Cermak is superior to Mr. Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, but you have said that he is superior to the military police and the civil authority in Knin; haven't you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said -- I have stated in my report that indeed General Cermak is superior to the military and the civilian police in Knin based on the documents that are included in that section where this topic is addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As part of your analysis in relation to these issues of authority, why didn't you include this information in your report for the Judges?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean these, these reports here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they show that indeed a civilian police official in the Zadar-Knin police administration, which is actually also covering an area outside the Knin Garrison, sends, indeed, information to the Ministry of Interior, but they do not allow to draw conclusions as to whether or not any information is shared by Mr. Cetina, in this case, with General Cermak. The fact that he is -- I mean, the fact that he's not included as an addressee in this report does not allow to draw any conclusions as to whether he receives information or not. We can only say he does not receive this report. We cannot draw other conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, there's another 40 or 50 behind in exactly the same terms. So it's not just this report. There's another 40 or 50. The Judges have them.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I meant the type of report. It's like a military sitrep. There is a list of addressees. It could be that some other people who are not included as -- on the list of addressees receive information that is included in these sitreps, probably not everything, through another chain. I'm not claiming, certainly not, that Mr. Cetina was providing information to Mr. Cermak. I'm just trying to explain why I did not use these type of documents in my report in the section on the authority or the position held by General Cermak while he was commander of the Knin Garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that because your report has been prepared exclusively with the aim of putting only one side of the case, that the negative in relation to Mr. Cermak did not suit the purposes of your argument for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The report deals, as it's explained in the scope, the report attempts to cover the role of General Gotovina, General Cermak, and General Markac during and after Operation Storm. I have tried to be as thorough as possible in describing that role. I did not consider it necessary to describe what they were not doing, because it's difficult to determine exactly where this starts and where this ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But if you are expressing an opinion, surely as an expert, you should be considering the other aspects as well, in the way that you're answering my questions by putting the other point of view for your side.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusions in the report are based on the information that I have reviewed. The references can be found in the footnotes. It is up to the reader to determine whether the conclusion I draw from the material I reviewed is correct or not. And it is obvious if I am confronted with other material that shows the opposite of my conclusions that I should be willing to review my conclusions and also change them. As I have attempted to explain with these documents, I think I'm open to do so, but I want to be as thorough as possible and also in this particular case explain why I didn't use these documents. I didn't use them because they, as you tried to put it, did not serve the goal of the report as you define the goal. In my view, the goal is different. It is to describe of role of certain people. Yeah, that concludes my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, may I try to see what Mr. Kay is seeking an answer to. He, as I understand it, put to you that you have used certain documents. You have explained to us that the documents you used are in the footnotes. Now, what he's asking you is other documents which perhaps do not -- are not contradicting your conclusions, but at least maybe by their number or their content are relevant to consider whether the impression gained by the documents you did use and you did put into your footnotes, whether it would not have been worth mentioning them. For example, to say there are 30 documents on this and this matter where one could ask oneself why no reference whatsoever is made to Mr. Cermak in this case to have them in your footnotes as well, because you say the reader, on the basis of the footnotes, can verify, can draw his own conclusions, but of course, only on the basis of the documents you did use. And the question by Mr. Kay is would it not have been -- would it not have given a more complete picture if you would have included the documents he draws your attention to at this moment also in the footnotes, even if they would not undermine your conclusions but at least to point at them. Would that not have been a better method?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours, there are documents which have been presented to me during cross-examination which I would really have liked to include to -- to avoid maybe certain mistakes, to be more complete on certain issues. I have not thought of including, for example, documents of the type we see now because I didn't consider them relevant in the context of determining or trying to establish the role, in this particular case, of General Cermak. Indeed, it could have been included, but as I said earlier when I was trying to describe the systems of sitreps, these particular types of documents, well, yes, they allow to conclude at that Mr. Cermak is not included in the list of addressees, but I would not be in a position to say, well, he should have been included or not. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But often you've told us that you would have expected something. Now, the question here then clearly is if -- and a similar question was put to you by Mr. Kay several times, whether you would not have expected to find a reference or copied the document to be copied to Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would certainly have expected that, and that's what I mentioned actually before the break, that if there were regular reports by the Civil Defence teams on the clearing activities, that information included in those reports would also have been sent to Mr. Cermak. If the Civil Defence teams were subordinated to him for the clearing activities. I have not stated in my report that the civil defence teams were subordinated to Mr. Cermak. I have only drawn a conclusion on the staff he establishes and the fact that members of the staff -- excuse me -- on the staff sanitation staff he establishes and that members of that staff report to him. I have not drawn any conclusions on Civil Defence except the ones I mentioned during my testimony this morning when I was confronted with Civil Defence documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The conclusion you have put forward to the Court, surely it's directly relevant to this, is that he is superior to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we are looking at civilian police documents.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we should -- we should be more precise. The conclusion I draw in relation to the authority of General Cermak over the civilian police is based on P510 which states that they have received -- I mean, the civilian police have received an order from General Cermak in relation to freedom of movement for civilians. There is also a document included -- there's also a document included in my report, and I will find it, where the -- an official of the civilian police in Knin asks, I believe, the head of the Zadar-Knin police administration to be allowed to participate in meetings between General Cermak and UNCRO in order to be informed immediately of decisions or agreements between General Cermak and UNCRO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was just about to see whether we could -- we can do two things. We could have an early break and then have a relatively long last session. We could also take a break for one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm going to change topics anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether that for transcription makes it any better, Mr. Kay, but apart from that, I at least appreciate that you would share my concern for the well-being of our transcriber this morning. Although it's not on the record, the transcriber tells us that she's okay, but I'll keep a close on you. Be assured of that. Then to have to transcribe this must be a very special experience. Mr. Kay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you were going to add some more because you're citing one of the sort of 12 orders again, I think.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was just going to add that the document I referred to at the end of my previous answer is D589, which is footnote 1043.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You go back to the same documents again in relation to this. Your Honour, I am going to change subjects. I've got it now. But we will turn to the military police, because with a swift glass of water, I'm sure I'll be okay. You were asked many questions by Mr. Misetic on the issue of Major Juric from the military police administration, the relationship with General Lausic, the chief of the military police administration. I'm not going to go over those details again, and for the Court's reference, Mr. Misetic has handled that cross-examination, and I'm not going to repeat matters, Your Honour, but let's just run through a few things. We know on the 5th of August, 1995, that a military police company was established in Knin by General Lausic's order as well as one in Benkovac, Drnis. We know that on the 5th of August, 1995, Exhibit P881, if we could look at that just for a moment, because this -- the reference to this order becomes important later on in relation to certain matters we're going to address. This is that order ending in 485 of 512, dated the 5th of August, from General Lausic to the 72nd in Split, referring to the successful completion of the Oluja military operation. We've seen this order before and we know that it refers again to the 72nd Military Police Battalion and to the military police company in Knin. Can we turn to page 2. For reference for questions to come, look at point 3. "A communications and reporting system shall be put in place immediately, in keeping with the system of reporting in the zones of responsibility of military police units." And 7: "For the execution of daily operations, the commanders of the newly established VP units shall be subordinated to the most senior military commander in their respective zone of responsibility." And we see to whom this order was addressed. Moving on from there, we know that the company was established, and various orders were issued to it in relation to the men on the 6th of August. If we can look at Exhibit D787, which is the front page of the daily order book of what was called then the Knin joint company, and again, it's just pointing out a few things that will become relevant further down the line. We see the stamp of the military post is 2233. Is that right, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that's the stamp to be used by the Knin joint company; is that right? It's the stamp of the 72nd being used by the Knin joint company?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the stamp of the 72nd. Now, I have seen stamps with additional characters behind the first four digits, whereby I thought -- I would think that these were stamps of sub-units, but I have never managed to establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We're not going to go through the book, but we're just pointing that out. Can we go to Exhibit D789. This is an order from -- it says Major Budimir, but Colonel Budimir who was the commander of the 72nd, on the 17th of August, and we notice there the order of the chief of military police of the 5th of August, ending in 485 that I asked us to pay attention to and why I selected it in the introduction, regarding the needs arising in the newly liberated areas of the Republic of Croatia, and it's an order that on the 17th of August to carry out the rotation of military and police forces from your units engaged in Knin, and it's to 1st Lieutenant Orsulic who is to be the Knin military police joint company commander, various other appointments under him. And then for the rotation in Knin, the commander of the 1st company provides 29 officers; the 2nd Company, 40; traffic company, 18; crime investigation military police department chief, duty service leader, and logistic platoon commander shall select rotation for their officers. We see various further details there. And if we turn over to page 2. Commander Budimir continues with the order that: Lists of people selected for rotation shall be committed to a Major and commanders of the aforementioned mentioned units are be responsible for the order. We can see here that it's delivered to the commander who is Mr. Lieutenant Orsulic, the 1st company of the military police Split, 2nd Company Split, 3rd Company Zadar, chief of crime, leader of operational duty, and the traffic company. General Cermak is not included within this order as someone to be in receipt of this information; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that General Cermak is not mentioned. Again from the military police point of view, there is no requirement to inform General Cermak or any other officer where this military police company is operating because it concerns purely military police, yeah, internal matters as to how they provide the manpower. One can expect that the commander of the company is going to introduce himself upon his arrival with the most senior HV officer in the area where his company is to operate and that then the matter of rotation is also notified to the most senior HV officer in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, if we see that 5th of August order, we know at point 7 that that was part of the command, and we also know that in point 3 that a communications and reporting system shall be put in place immediately in keeping with the system of reporting in the zones of responsibility. First of all, was this a document you were familiar with when you wrote your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This specific one for the rotation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And it would have been useful as additional information, but -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Secondly, General Cermak would have been included within this document if -- if Lieutenant Orsulic of the Knin military police was to report to him so that he knew who his military police subordinate was to be. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, it's a purely military police internal order dealing with the internal organisation and activities of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. The commander Lieutenant Orsulic will know from the instructions he has received from Colonel Budimir, and again, from what was mentioned in the order by General Lausic on the establishment of the companies, I believe P881, that he is to be subordinated for the regular or the daily military police tasks to the most senior HV officer in the area, and it is then, as I mentioned, up to the commander of the military police unit that is to go to that area to introduce himself with the most senior HV officer, in this case General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Firstly, you've incorrectly stated what the rules are under Regulation 9, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to P881, but we can go to the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Regulation 9 of the rules states the most senior commander by function, and that was something that I brought to your attention earlier in my cross-examination as something that you had not correctly described in your evidence and report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think the issue was that Mr. Theunens relied on an earlier incorrect translation, which was then later corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's my point, that you've put yourself forward as an expert, but you didn't have the right translation of the rules, so your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- Mr. Waespi, I think let's keep it in neutral terms, that is that Mr. Kay did not blame specifically perhaps Mr. Theunens for having relied upon the wrong translation but establishes that that was the case, and that maybe relevant for his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. If you would like to see Article 9 again in the revised translation of the OTP document, Exhibit P880, page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Theunens will accept that the language you just used was the -- was the valid translation at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He asked to see it, Your Honour, which is why I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that -- I don't recall saying that I wanted to see it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's not -- if you don't, if you feel no need to see it, let's proceed. If you feel that need, Mr. Kay will ask it to be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. You said, "We can go to the rules," so I'm taking us to the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there are several ways of doing that, either looking at them or quoting them. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So do you accept it from me that that was the correct translation that was issued in the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Ah, we're there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can see it, Mr. Theunens. This is a corrected translation from the original OTP documents, because it concerns the issue of the highest HV commander by function.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, and, in my view, it doesn't change -- it doesn't imply any significant changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It does, doesn't it, because the function of the officer is critical to the relevance of the subordination.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In theory -- I mean, you can imagine scenarios where that does, indeed, play a role, but looking again at the material we are reviewing, unless you're going to give me examples where it has an importance that is by function is added, I don't believe that it changes anything to what has been established so far in my report or, for example, when Mr. Misetic was cross-examining me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Say you have a colonel-general of the Education Corps, and he happens, because of his distinguished academic career, to hold that rank, and he's in the armed forces, and he's running the education department in the area, you don't report to him in relation to your duties, do you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends how you define running, because if he is the commander of a military training centre or a school where for whatever reason there is a requirement to use military police or to have military police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think what I considered symptomatic earlier happens here again. We're now dwelling into areas -- Mr. Kay put to you that -- that it may be significant, the difference between a highest HV commander or highest HV commander by function. If the highest commander is not functioning in the, could I say, operational command structure, then -- and that's what Mr. Kay put to you, then it may make a difference. Have I understood your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you could please answer that or comment on that, rather than to dwell in military police getting lost in educational institutions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I mean the operational command structure, we know that the garrison commander does not -- plays no role in the operational chain of command. However, the garrison commander is responsible for order and discipline in the area covered by the garrison, i.e., the area outside the barracks. He will need resources in order to fulfill that responsibility, and we have seen documents, including those included in my report, whereby the garrison commander makes use of the military police in order to fulfill his responsibility of maintaining order and discipline, even if as a garrison commander he's not part of the operational chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to see if I understood your answer correctly. What you say is a garrison commander that may be functional in view of his responsibility to maintain order and discipline, that he may be functional in the context of Article 9 in relation to troops or officers who are not directly and organically subordinated to him. Is that more or less a proper understanding of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we are dealing with the relation between a garrison commander and military police unit in his -- in the area covered by the garrison. I think what Mr. Kay was pointing at was you can have, indeed, a colonel-general who is not a commander, because he may be a professor or he may be a chief of staff, and there, of course, the clarification of Article 9 is -- is important. But in the context of the garrison commander, we are talking about somebody who is a commander, at least according to the regulations, even though he's outside the operational chain of command, and that's why I tried to explain the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In fact, it's described as a non-operational post under Regulation 2 of the organisation. I'll get the exhibit number for us. It is D3 -- D34, paragraph 2, exhibit -- paragraph 2 of Exhibit D34, Organisational order regarding work, order, and discipline at garrison HQs. "The garrison headquarters commands do not have an operational function and the right to issue orders to Croatian army units except precisely prescribed authorities regarding work, order, and discipline at the garrison," et cetera. Point 7 of the 5th of August order by General Lausic does not cause the military police to report under point 7 to the garrison commander or whomsoever for their daily tasks, does it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we see point 7 of the 5th of August order again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Please. It is in Exhibit P881, and it says: "For the execution of daily operations, the commanders of the newly established VP units shall be subordinated to the most senior Croatian army commander in their respective zone of responsibility." So it's quite clear that that is not, through point 7, a subordination to the garrison commander, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the garrison commander is the most senior HV commander in the zone of responsibility of the Knin Garrison for the matters he is responsible for, i.e., maintaining order and discipline as well as other aspects covered in Article 54 of D32, as well as D34.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But it refers to the daily operations in respect of which the military police for their daily operations are not subordinate to the garrison commander. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We are talking about -- I mean, the daily operations here are daily operations conducted by military police which, if I remember well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You cited Article 10 which -- as being daily operations. Mr. Misetic disagreed with you in relation to that, and I agree with his cross-examination of you, by the way, on that matter, but Article 10 means that the garrison commander, by your argument, is suddenly taking on all the responsibilities there are nothing to do with him. If we look at the military rules governing structure and operation of the military police. Which by your argument would mean that as a matter of coincidence the garrison commander would be taking over all the responsibility in relation to the military police which would include fighting, sabotage, terrorist, rebels, carrying out combat tasks on the front line, security of the president, verification, detection, dispatch and escort of members. The Croatian army have abandoned their unit. He wouldn't be doing much garrison commanding, would he? He would be running the whole show if your argument was -- was right, Mr. Theunens. He would be, Isn't that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Article 10 lists the duties the military police can do. I think it's clear from the article that they're not -- the military police is not carrying out all these duties at the same time by one and the same unit. A military police company of, I don't know, 150 or maybe 300 men would not be in a position to carry out all these duties listed here from 1 to 10 at the same time in the same area. The comment made by Mr. Kay about participation in combat tasks, which is listed in paragraph 9 of Article 10, clearly states that these tasks can only be carried out, i.e., participation in carrying out combat tasks pursuant to an order by the minister of defence of the Republic of Croatia. Carrying out combat tasks implies that the operational chain of command is working and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've taken one. Take eight then. Go on. Sabotage, terrorist, rebels, and other enemy groups.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there are sabotage units in the area covered by the garrison, there will obviously be a coordination between -- or cooperation between the command of the military district, the garrison commander and others as to see how they can deal with it. It is indeed logical that taking into account that the responsibility of the garrison commander is mainly territorial and that he is responsible for the common facilities that are used in the garrison or -- and order and discipline there, whereas the dealing or the action against sabotage and terrorist units will consist of conducting combat tasks, that there the role of the garrison commander can only be maybe to provide information as these sabotage units may have done something against the common facility, but he will not be involved in the chain of command of the struggle against these terrorist and sabotage units. And again for your information, the Special Police sends reports on the discovery of members or alleged members of the former Serb forces they discovered during their search operations in the territory covered by the Knin garrison to the commander of the Knin garrison, and that is discussed in the section on Special Police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, may I ask you in relation to that last answer, were you referring to such reporting in a broader sense, or were you talking about, if I could say, the nine we discussed yesterday, because for the nine, we have -- at least there is evidence of a very specific context as we dealt with yesterday in quite some detail and where you said you were not familiar with that context. Is it any broader, or were you referring to the reporting on the nine who had been found where Mr. Roberts was around as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is broader, Your Honour, and I will check for the correct references because I made a distinction in my report between the provision of information on such groups, on one hand, and the actual hand-over of the people, which refers to the nine, on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Special Police are under the Ministry of Interior. They are nothing to do with the military. You should know that, Mr. Theunens. You do know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but I tried to explain why or what the possible role of a garrison commander could be in the context of the participation, the fight against sabotage, terrorist, rebel, and other enemy groups. And it has nothing to do with the military police either, but I just focused on the aspect of sabotage, terrorists, and rebels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could you please give answers that focus on the issue instead of widening it far way beyond what it needs and keep it relevant to the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A break, yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, time for the break. We will have a break, and we will resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Going back to Exhibit D789, please, and page 2 of that document. A fundamental principle of command, Mr. Theunens, is that people have to know who they are commanded by and who is under their command. Don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if your argument is right, this document emanating from the commander of the 72nd as to who is in charge of the military police, traffic police, what the rotation is, when they are to arrive, is all information that the garrison commander would have to know if these units and this company were subordinated to him. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He will need some of these elements. I mean the garrison commander will need some of these elements, but they will be communicated in another manner than through an order which is purely dealing with internal military police and matters going from the military police battalion commander to his company commanders. It would not be efficient to bother somebody with outside the chain, the military police professional chain with certain issues or certain aspects that are included in this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's complete nonsense, isn't it? This would be information that the garrison commander, if your argument is right, would have to know. He'd have to know whom he was commanding.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we please see the first page of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go through it. He'd have to know there was a rotation on the 17th of August. Yes?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Or he would have to be informed in advance at least as a matter of courtesy, but also for operational requirements it would be important for the garrison commander to be inform that indeed the rotation is taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're not talking about matters of courtesy here. We are talking about subordination, Mr. Theunens, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but just to clarify the issue, subordination in the sense of Article 9 of 1994 rules on the use of military police, P880.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And for clarification, that is not in the heading of this document, is it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The document refers to the -- the order of the 5th of August, but we have seen it there in paragraph 7, Article 9 is reiterated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, it's not actually. It's written in a different form. It doesn't include the words "by function." But people can see that for themselves. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if I'm allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It would be unusual at least from a military point of view to change subordination relations that have been established or confirmed in a regulation in 1994, to suddenly start to change them when a significant military operation is being conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't know how that helps us, but let's go -- go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, these are comments we can do without.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He would have to know who was in charge of the traffic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I mean, if he, the garrison commander, needs assistance from one of these sections or components of the company, the logical procedure would be to contact the company commander, and the company commander can indeed inform the garrison or any other commander about the composition of his forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They would need to know who they reported to, and if it's the garrison commander, that's not in here, is it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- who do you mean "they would need to know?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Orsulic would have to be told, "You are reporting to the garrison commander." We've seen that in many orders. It's not here, is it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not here, but based on the introduction and the fact that we're the 17th of August, by then, people in the area, I mean at least in the military, know who is holding which position where, but I mean more importantly the introduction of the order, there is no requirement, at least from the military point of view, to specify that the Knin -- that the commander of the Knin company has to report to -- to General Cermak. It's self-explicatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where? Where?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of what I have explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But where is it self-explicatory? Let's say Lieutenant Orsulic, and this is his first post as the commander of the Knin military police. How does he know where to go and who to see and who to report to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knows in theory who, I mean, he has to contact, not the individual, I mean the name, but who by position by going to Knin. He will have been briefed by Colonel Budimir, and he would also, if nobody has told him that it is General Cermak who is the commander of the garrison in Knin, well, then, Lieutenant Orsulic will collect or find out that information prior to going with his people to Knin. But you're right, it's not specified in this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It tells them where they must be present, the time, about transport.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and these are things that are not of a -- there is no need to know for the operational commander or the most senior HV commander by function to know how these people -- where they will gather, at what time, and how they will travel to -- to Knin. The most important is that there is a continuous presence of military police, and this is an internal order in the military police battalion to ensure this continuous presence of military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You slipped up there, because you said the operational commander or the most senior HV commander by function. When you first gave evidence about these matters in this court, you described the operational commander.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Under Article 9.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. Others can look at it.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are other documents connected with this which are the orders, and what we will do is we will look at them, and we'll look at a following document just so that we can see the detail of what is given. If we could look at 2D07-0590.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, when we are waiting for this document to be shown, when you said others can look at it, I don't know who you had in mind, but it included the Chamber, and, if so, some assistance in where to look exactly would certainly be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't want to spend all my time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you, but you could in one way or another assist us to know where exactly to find that instead of -- I mean, it takes just as much time for us to find it as it will take you. You put it to the witness, and you suggest that he said something, and, of course, we'd like to verify. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're looking now at an order that was issued by Commander Budimir to the 1st Company, giving that 29 military police officers, telling them when to assemble. We will now look at the next document concerning the 2nd Company --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D1062.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1062 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 2D07-0592. This is still coming up, but it's the order to the 2nd Company and all the details. If we turn to page 2, we see it's from captain Dzolic which the Court knows is a witness earlier in the proceedings. Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D1063.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1063 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go to 2D07-0596. This is a document from the traffic police company, dated the 17th of August, detailing their officers who are going to comply with the order that was issued and citing the 485 of 5th of August order. Again we don't need to go into the detail, but, Your Honour, could this be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D1064, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit D1064 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document is 2D07-0552. This is a document from Major Cipcic of the traffic police company who signed the previous order, dated the 17th of August. It goes to the commander, Colonel Budimir. Sorry, it goes to the assistant commander for the traffic, Major Cipcic, from 1st Lieutenant Renic, and it's the list of duty service staff for the work in the duty service of the joint independent Knin company, and it's pursuant to a meeting held on the 12th of August by the 72nd, by which the duty service is to appoint a representative of the duty service leader of the Knin Company in the transition period and in line with the first order from Commander Budimir we saw, and we see the people who are to be used to set up the duty service. Staff members will rotate in shifts according to the given schedule, assume the duty to represent the duty service leader, et cetera, and the selection of the shift leaders and information concerning that. May this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D1065, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1065 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Looking at that last document, wouldn't it have been relevant for the commander of the garrison, if your argument is right, to have been copied in on this document so he knew who duty service staff were who were going to be working in Knin and subordinate to him?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would indeed be useful for the garrison commander to know who the duty officer is in the military police, but he will be informed of that through another document. He may receive, for example, a duty roster which includes only the information he needs to have instead of all these kind of purely internal military police information dealing with internal functioning of the military police. There's no need to know for the operational commander or the most senior HV officer by duty of all these kind of internal information. It's only distractive for him. Distractive, I'm not sure whether it's an English word, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would distract his attention from more important matters; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is there anywhere the duty roster that you talk about, have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen such duty roster. I have seen it in other environments but not for Knin and General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you've seen them elsewhere but not for Knin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the witness just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just digesting that, Your Honour. I'm sorry I repeated it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We heard it, and we were able to digest it already. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to Knin, then, is that a document that you have looked for?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I have done searches on -- on these issues. I'll keep it short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a large number of these rotations, including the exact same constructions, none of which include General Cermak within the documents. I don't propose, with the Court's consent, to go through each and every one to make the same point as I anticipate what the witness's answers are, but I am not just producing one document on the matter. There are a whole file here which I would propose to file by bar table means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I take it these documents do not appear in the footnotes of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wonder, but I'm not the master of the time of Mr. Theunens. The way to proceed would be and that would be fair to him to provide him with copies of these documents and invite him to read them. He now knows what the issue is, and then to ask him, perhaps after the weekend, to ask him whether this triggers any need for comment other than he has already given in response to your questions, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. These are Prosecution documents that I am holding in my hand. They're all their documents, rather than mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not -- the only thing is that we know the answers that the witness reviewed, a couple of them. I have not reviewed them. The witness was not in a position to review them. If they are all approximately the same, then I would expect he comes back after the weekend to say that he has no comments other than he had before the weekend, and then that seems fair to me and to both the Prosecution and the Defence and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it we will find ways of getting copies of these documents to the witness through the victims' and witness' section. May I take it these are not yet on the first three bar table submissions, so we expect a fourth one, including these.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But I do want to ask a question about it. As to whether you'd seen these documents before, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did. I'm not a hundred per cent sure, but I'm sure I did not include them in my report for the reasons I explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You didn't include them in your report, and they arise as a result of for RFA's, requests for assistance. So did you review those documents?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered the question. I believe seen them. I mean, I don't check systematically how they were obtained by the OTP; that would lead me too far, but I have looked at them and based on the comments on the reply I gave earlier, I did not consider them relevant for my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We will deal with it that way according to Your Honour's suggestion, and we will now turn to another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Kay, I have to ask the witness whether he has objections. I started saying I'm not a master of your time, Mr. Theunens. When I'm talking about the weekend, of course, it starts only at 5.00, but I don't know whether you have other things to do, and I just wanted to seek your agreement with this procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My Supreme Commander has booked a weekend to Paris before we started with testimony, but we come back on sunday, and she will understand that on Monday, when it's a UN holiday, I can look at this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This sheds specific light on command and control, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's turn to Exhibit D790.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And while this is coming up, I while this is coming up, I will put the broad proposition of what this is, Mr. Theunens, so you know, and it accords with Mr. Misetic's cross-examination of you that, in fact, what happened here was that the commander of the 72nd Budimir maintained control of the independent Knin company, and it wasn't handed over to anyone else, that they remained subordinated to him at all times. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it -- I would consider -- I mean, I'm reading the document but I'm listening to what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the application of Articles 8 and 9 with the professional line and the operational line. Articles 8 and 9 of P880.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, here we have an example, 22nd of August, 1995. The safety of the Knin command post, we know that to mean garrison, Commander Colonel General Cermak needing security, and an order is made by Colonel Kozic of the military police administration to the commander of the 72nd Battalion that he will conduct all organisational preparations to take over the security of the Knin garrison commander from the Knin military police 7th Company. It says military post, vonja posta, but vonja policija is what it means, of the 7th Company. Now, this indicates, does it not, that General Cermak didn't have the authority to order Lieutenant Orsulic, the commander of the Knin 7th Company, to provide for his security, as he was not subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but there are several, I mean, as I said, possibilities in this context, because it could be that -- it could indeed be that General Cermak has asked for security by military police. We don't know where he asked it. Maybe he did order Orsulic to provide security, and Orsulic said, I don't do it. I have included in my report P509, P513, P512, which are examples of orders by General Cermak to the military police in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've looked at those, the UNCRO vehicle ones, et cetera, et cetera. Let's deal with this. Please don't throw up the UNCRO orders, but look at this, please, because security is a regular task of the military police; is it not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security in general, yes, but I'm just checking in the Article 10 whether anything specific is said about ensuring personal security, because I understand that these people functioned as kind of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the very first one, actually, of Article 10. "The protection of life and the personal security of military personnel and other Croatian republic citizens and the protection of their property." So it's Article 1 -- point 1 of Article 10 of Exhibit P880, the Rules Of The Military Police. Now, by your argument that you've put to the Court that General Cermak had the military police subordinated to him, he would have been able to ordered this. It didn't need to go up to the military police administration, did it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of this document is that it deals with a very specific aspect of security, i.e., providing personal security on what appears to be a 24/7 basis to the garrison commander, which will obviously have implications on who can provide that security. You need specialised personnel. You need sufficient personnel in order to have them present or available on a 24/7 basis. So in my view it goes beyond the execution of regular or daily military police tasks as is explained in Article 9 of P880 and reiterated in the order by Lausic of the 5th of July. I believe P881, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you agree that the order does not specify any special policemen that would be required, it just says from the formation of the military police forces of the Knin Company?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article -- excuse me. Paragraph 2 does not really indicate -- I agree with you that they have to have specific training, but there is mention made of appropriate equipment and weapons, so that would mean they would need to know how to operate these weapons, and as is stated there "maximally paying attention to the image and behaviour." I don't know what is specifically is meant by that. Military policemen should know how to behave and which image to maintain. So it could be that the intention is expressed to -- to make a specific selection of specific personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All of which could have been dealt with by Mr. Orsulic himself because he has all those people we've seen in the orders we've just looked at coming under his command to Knin; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not a specialist or an expert in the domain of ensuring personal security, but I have spoken with people, for example, in that area and you need a lot of people to ensure a 24/7 personal protection of an individual. I don't think it can just be solved by -- by a company, because this company is there also to -- or carry out the regular military police tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You'd agree, though, it does defy your analysis on the subordination issue; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, because I see this as a very specific task, ensuring personal security or personal safety of a -- of a colonel-general, of a senior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us look at Exhibit D791. This is a report dated the 21st of August, 1995, from Lieutenant Orsulic of the Knin Company concerning securing a Ministry of Defence working group during their tour of military facilities with two military policemen and reporting to the military administration. No report there to the -- General Cermak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: By your argument there should have been a report to General Cermak, shouldn't there?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it depends whether General Cermak had imposed this task or not. If he had imposed this task, then there surely should have been a report to General Cermak. If he had not imposed this task, then there is not necessarily a report to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So if General Cermak has imposed no tasks, we will see no reports from Lieutenant Orsulic to him. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reports on the execution of those specific tasks, yes, that would be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you seen any reports from Lieutenant Orsulic as the commander of the Knin Company to General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not seen such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit -- well, number 2D07-0053. This is dated the 16th of September, 1995. It comes from Colonel Kozic again from the military police administration to the deputy chief of military police administration, Brigadier Biskic, and is a general assessment of the security situation in the Republic of Croatia since Storm, and "According to our assessment, the security situation," he describes within the area of responsibility of the military police units, and he describes it as being good and stable, operating jointly in the entire territory. Military police and forces of the MUP alongside with military and civilian authorities set up, have taken control of the area. We can see the rest of the text about VP units. Breaches of general security and public order by way of offences, referring to the breaches of public order, and the overall activities undertaken. If we turn to page 2. A recommendation about abandoning the system of work and switching in another way, intensive -- start with intensive familiarisation of HV commanders, et cetera. We can see the text there. This indicates a high degree of observation and control by the military police administration, does it not, of its units in the liberated area?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it is coherent with Article 9 -- excuse me, Article 8. Yeah, sorry. Article 8 of P880.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And the structure of the system and the reports that exist show the system working within a reporting system, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed according to the -- or in accordance with the professional line as explained earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May that document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D1066, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D14066 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at 2D07-0079. This is a document dated the 21st of September, again from -- it says Commander Lieutenant Michael Budimir here which is probably not the correct translation of his rank. To Lieutenant Orsulic, and it concerns taking away of objects, and it's ordered that that is forbidden, that the commander of the joint company, Lieutenant Orsulic, is responsible for carrying out that order. So it's concerned with the taking away of war booty. No copy of this being sent to General Cermak to advise him of the position with the Knin Company?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that this document is not sent to General Cermak, but we should have a look at the -- the order that lays at the basis of this order, i.e., the order by General Gotovina of the 13th of September, which is mentioned in the introduction, in order to see whether that one was sent to General Cermak, because this document, to me, indicates that General Gotovina's order is forwarded through the chain of command from the highest level to the lowest level, to the various units, and in that context it would be unusual to have the commander of the military police battalion send the order to one of the garrison commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't have that to hand, but we will try and locate that within the next few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D1067.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1067 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are several other documents of a similar nature which I will bar table to save time, and the Court is familiar with the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are. I just wonder, I don't know how many there are, and I don't want to burden --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Not a great deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not a great deal. If there's just a few, if you -- if there's anyway to add them to the collection already prepared for Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We'll endeavour to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And there are only a few, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can be a relative concept, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us go to a document now which is 65 ter 2562. And this precursors a large number of similar documents of which we will be dealing with the first lot. The remainder are untranslated. They have been provided by the Prosecution as quite a great deal of them, but they tell the same story, and it concerns the daily report for the 31st of August, 1995. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no specific recollection of this document, but I have seen similar military police reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before we break for the day, I want to go through the document with you. It's a duty service report from the military police, the 72nd. You can see the date of it. The first heading is "Breaches of the provisions of the Rules of Military Discipline." And you will notice in the first point that on the 31st of August, a member of the -- of a particular unit, VP there, meaning military police post, 1108 in Drnis, entered the premises of the 72nd Military Police Post in Knin and reported that at a certain time in a neighbourhood in Knin, three members of the Croatian army driving a car had stolen a large amount of furniture from the house and a patrol of the 72nd Military Police in Knin was sent to investigate, and that the patrol noticed the vehicle in front of the Split Garrison command and brought those persons in the vehicle to the military police in Knin. And then the story unfolds over what happens. Let us move to page 2. And we can see that the daily report for this day includes a report from the Knin police station about a Croatian army member and an issue with a member of the public and a patrol of the 72nd in Knin was sent out, put as VP 2233, meaning the Knin Company, and we can see further details there about the military police in Knin. If we go to page 3, these are all headings, general headings that we've seen of breaches of the Rules of Military Discipline, other events, securing public gatherings. Page 3 has attacks on officials of the military police. Further up the page in English, means of coercion, breaches of provisions of the Rules of Military Discipline, safety of traffic. And then we can go to the next page, page 4. We see further information about other -- other military police activity, including a patrol of the military police 72nd in Drnis, but of interest is who this is delivered to. First of all, the Military Police Administration Operative Duty department. That's general Lausic's department, isn't it, up in the headquarters in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a department within General Lausic's administration, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Next the commander of the Split Military District. Number 3 is the commander of the Split Military Garrison.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Split garrison, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. SIS, being the information service, chief of Split Dalmatia police administration, military court, military Prosecutor's office, commander for operations and training, duty officer of the 72nd, and the chief of the military crime police. No Knin garrison included, Mr. Theunens. But do you recollect seeing this document at all?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you asked me that already. I have seen similar documents, and it is correct that here there is -- I mean, there is no mention made of the command of the Knin Garrison, where I would expect -- I mean, based on the first incident that is reported, which took place in Knin or was reported in Knin, that such reports should also be sent to the commander of the Knin Garrison, as according to the regulations, he's responsible for maintaining order and discipline in his garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the reporting line from the duty service here does not include him within this document, and we've seen a number of incidents concerning Knin which, if your argument was correct, he would be informed about; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. I explained -- I mean, independent of what you call my argument, I explained that I considered that this report should also have been sent to the commander of the Knin Garrison. It has actually nothing to do with subordination or not. It is a matter of the commander of the garrison having information, operational information, he needs in order to carry out his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to ask the last question on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one question then, because I need two minutes for another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I should have announced that so no need to apologise. One question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's this issue I've been putting to you, and there are more of these, all going to the Split Garrison instead of Knin. There are a whole batch, which indicates, does it not, that, in fact, the Knin Company was acting under the 72nd and was not working with and reporting to the Knin Garrison?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have answered that question. I have explained that General Cermak has issued a number of orders to the Knin military police. I have also explained that the reporting of incidents in the zone of responsibilities of a garrison is not necessarily related to command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll continue with these documents with the Court's leave, on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D1068, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1068 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Theunens, I need two minutes for a procedural matter which doesn't concern you in any way. First of all, I'd like to express my appreciation that you accepted the invitation to look at a few documents. They will be delivered to you through the usual channels. We'll not sit on Monday. We will resume on the 9th of December, that's Tuesday, at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. We'd like to see you back. My instructions in relation to not to speak with anyone about the testimony matter already given or still to be given remains the same as it always was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Further to that matter, if we send the documents through e-court, Mr. Theunens has access to e-court, and that apparently is a much more efficient way of getting them to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have access to e-court. I'm just thinking of how can I identify the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They have descriptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's take care that we use the usual channels to make sure that -- apart from that, it would burden Mr. Theunens printing them out. If he wants to take them with him, then, of course, that would not be very reasonable that he would have to do the job which is supposed to be done by others. Mr. Theunens, thank you very much. We would like to see you back on Tuesday. Madam Usher, could you escort Mr. Theunens out the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go, we are Tuesday afternoon for Mr. Theunens benefit. I believe we are in the afternoon on Tuesday, not in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just a moment. Earlier I said I think the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
